lessons.title: What College Really Costs
objectives: Compute cost of attendance and net price.
lessons.hook: Two schools: $31,000 and $68,000 sticker prices. Which is cheaper? Reveal aid offers.

notes.body: Tuition, fees, housing, food, books, transportation, personal.
Categorize every line: gift, earned, loan (and whose loan).

discussion: Why might the sticker price mislead families?
reflection: What questions would you ask a college’s financial aid office?
lessons.extension: Use a college’s net price calculator with a fictional family profile.
lessons.realWorld: Every college must post a net price calculator on its website.

lessons.title: Student Loans and Repayment
objectives: Calculate student-loan payments and total interest.
Explain subsidized vs. unsubsidized loans and capitalization.
lessons.hook: “I’ll worry about loans after graduation.” What could go wrong?

notes.body: Use the installment formula; standard federal plan is 10 years.
Unpaid interest added to principal increases future interest.
Payments around 10% of gross income or less are often considered manageable.

discussion: How might loan payments affect other life goals?
misconceptions: Discuss interest accrual and collection consequences.
reflection: What is the most you would be willing to borrow, and why?
lessons.extension: Research income-driven repayment plans on studentaid.gov.
lessons.realWorld: Federal loan rates are set each year; private loans vary by credit.

lessons.title: Comparing Career Earnings
objectives: Include forgone earnings and costs in comparisons.
lessons.hook: Graph: degree vs. apprenticeship cumulative earnings. Where do the lines cross?

notes.body: Earnings − education costs − loan payments over time.
Salaries vary by region, field, and person.

reflection: What matters to you in a career beyond pay?
lessons.extension: Use the Decision Lab “College & Career ROI Explorer”.

extend: Find the year when cumulative earnings cross.

lessons.realWorld: The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists median pay and outlook by occupation.

lessons.title: Payback and ROI of Education
lessons.hook: Claim: “College is always worth it.” Students sort evidence cards into support/refute.

notes.body: Completion rates, job placement, and debt load.
Interest and aptitude affect success and earnings.

discussion: Why might two students choose differently with the same data?
reflection: Which pathway are you considering, and what is its ROI?
lessons.extension: Research a real program’s completion rate on the College Scorecard.
lessons.realWorld: The federal College Scorecard reports costs, debt, and earnings by program.

front.title: Loan payment
front.html:
⟨D=\dfrac{Pi}{1-(1+i)^{-N}}⟩
P = balance dollars when repayment begins; i = monthly decimal interest rate; N = monthly payments; D = monthly dollars.
⟨i=\tfrac{r}{12}⟩; r = annual interest rate.
Use the repayment balance, not just original borrowing; unpaid interest or fees may add to it.
Fixed-rate model; at zero interest, ⟨D=\tfrac{P}{N}⟩.

front.title: Four-year borrowing model
front.text: Assume $5,500 each year for 4 years, no fees or in-school interest; then 6.5% over 120 months.

front.title: Interest & completion
head: Term
Meaning / quick example
rows: Borrower may receive an interest subsidy during eligible periods.
Interest generally accrues while in school.
Unpaid interest added to principal under loan terms.
Costs and debt may remain even without the credential.

back.title: Which pathway pays back?
back.text: Certificate costs $12,000 and adds $6,000 yearly earnings. Degree costs $40,000 and adds $10,000. Same baseline; ignore tax, raises and financing.
back.example: Simple payback = cost ÷ annual earnings gain.

back.title: Sooner vs. larger return
back.html:
The certificate wins on speed in that model. Over 10 working years after completion:
Certificate: $60,000 gain − $12,000 = $48,000.
Degree: $100,000 gain − $40,000 = $60,000.
The degree has a larger modeled 10-year gain. Different completion times, job placement, missed earnings or personal goals can reverse the choice.

back.title: Count opportunity cost
back.html:
Economic education cost = net price + earnings forgone + financing costs, using a consistent baseline.
Two years with $20,000 yearly earnings forgone plus $15,000 total net price:
⟨2(20{,}000)+15{,}000=55{,}000⟩
$55,000 before financing costs
Subtract earnings while studying. Count only living-cost differences if baseline costs are already included.

back.title: Earnings with steady raises
back.html:
⟨S=a\dfrac{(1+g)^n-1}{g}⟩
a = first-year earnings dollars; g = annual decimal raise; n = earning years; S = total nominal earnings.
$40,000 first year, 3% yearly raises, 3 years:
$40,000 + $41,200 + $42,436
$123,636 total
At zero raises: ⟨S=an⟩. No unemployment, tax or discounting in this model.

back.title: Before committing
items: Compare net price across all years, not only year one.
Check completion, transfer-credit and job-placement outcomes for the actual program.
Estimate realistic local earnings, not only a national high salary.
Compare apprenticeship, certificate, transfer and direct-to-work routes.
Model affordable payments using expected take-home pay.
Check whether aid requires a GPA, enrollment level or annual application.

back.title: Reminders & mistakes
good: Use multiple earnings and completion scenarios.
Loan payments compete with rent and other needs.
bad: Borrowing below salary is always safe
compare gift aid and net price.

questions.prompt: Riley is admitted to Lakeview Private College: tuition and fees $46,500, housing and food $12,600, books/transportation/personal $2,800.
